newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWEDISH POLICE PROBE S.AFRICAN LINK TO PALME.
newsitem.headline: SWEDISH POLICE PROBE S.AFRICAN LINK TO PALME.

text.p: Detectives trying to unlock the mystery of Swedish prime minister Olof Palme's murder said on Thursday a possible link to a South African spy could be a fresh lead in the unsolved 10-year-old murder.

Police investigating the 1986 murder of Palme said some allegations by Eugene De Kock that South Africa's previous white minority government could be involved in the killing were new to the commission.
"A part of the De Kock information is new. I do not want to say what is new to us and what is not," Lars Jonsson, deputy of the police investigation, told the national news agency TT.
"We have included reports similar to these about South Africa in our investigation but I am unable to say what they are," TT quoted Jonsson as saying.

De Kock, former chief of a covert South African police hit squad, told a court that an apartheid spy was involved in the murder of Palme and the killing was a "project" of Craig Williamson known as "Operation Long Reach".
Williamson was one of the white minority government's most effective spies during the 1970s and 1980s and has admitted to carrying out bombings and other actions against anti-apartheid activists.
Operation Long Reach was a secret programme by the apartheid government to harass or silence its opponents abroad.
Jonsson would not comment on any possible investigation of de Kock, but said speculation about Williamson emerged within a year or so of the murder, TT reported.
"We expect to receive some of the information through the Foreign Ministry. Then we will examine it and compare it with what we knew earlier," TT quoted him as saying.

De Kock, a colonel in the apartheid-era police, made the allegations while testifying in mitigation of sentence before the judge who convicted him last month of six murders and a series of other crimes.
Swedish investigations have never publicly revealed any South African link, preferring to dwell on a possible Kurdish connection alleged involve extreme Kurdish nationalists.
Palme was shot dead by a single bullet to the back as he was walking home from the cinema in central Stockholm with his wife Lisbet on February 28, 1986.

In the early days of the investigation dozens of theories emerged, including a conspiracy of Swedish police and right-wing businessmen but none of the 18,000 leads of the past decade have solved the crime.
More than 300 detectives initially took part in the inquiry but only a handful of officers are now involved and police sources say the investigation is due to be permanently shelved early next year.
Police arrested and tried a man identified by Palme's widow as the killer but the case was dismissed for lack of evidence.
The man, Christer Pettersson, always denied any involvement in the murder and was cleared in 1989 when a Stockholm appeals court overturned a guilty verdict delivered by a lower court.
The murder weapon has never been found.
